newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Severn outlines buyback impact.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Severn outlines buyback impact.

text.p: British water and sewerage company Severn Trent Plc expects gearing to rise to around 35 percent after it completes a planned share buyback, finance director Alan Costin said on Tuesday.
"After the share buyback, we would expect to see (gearing) up to the mid-30 percent," Costin told Reuters in a telephone interview. As of end-March, the level was 27.4 percent.
Severn Trent said it intended to complete a buyback of up to 10 percent of shares announced last year, after buying 5.6 percent in December.
Costin pointed out that the impact of a one-off tax on excess profits proposed by the new Labour government would be on top of that forecast.
He added that interest cover should be six times after the buyback operation, which awaits approval from the annual meeting.

Severn Trent said year pre-tax profits rose to 391 million stg from 373 million previously, excluding a 20 million provision for restructuring, and paid out a dividend of 36.5 pence per share, up from 32.37 pence.
Chief executive Vic Cocker said the 12.8 percent rise in the dividend was partly attributable to a strong performance at the company's non-regulated businesses.
"A lot (of the dividend growth) is fuelled by the non-regulated businesses," he said, adding that they accounted for around 30-40 percent of the increase in dividend.
Cocker said non-regulated businesses, such as the group's waste management arm Biffa, had contributed some 42 percent of growth in operating profits in the year.
He said profits in non-regulated activities had grown 28 percent in the year ending March 31 and the company aimed to see 20 percent growth per year in the future.
"Certainly we should be able to grow them at 20 percent per year," he said.

Cocker said that in Biffa, Severn Trent would like to maintain levels of improvement seen since 1993, which was "a good, steady record of growth...and we intend to maintain that sort of scale of increase."
He said in the waste management business, the focus was on organic growth but the company would look at small to medium-sized acquisitions if they were viable.
